Barriers

Why AI cannot simply be switched on

1. Opacity

We do not know how the model reached its recommendation, so the anesthesiologist cannot explain it.

2. Liability

If the AI decides wrongly, it is hard to say who is responsible.

3. Bias

A model trained mainly on adults will not be accurate for children. Training data must be diverse.

4. Over-reliance

Doctors may trust AI over their own judgment. Patients change quickly, so the anesthesiologist must still decide independently.

Schematic illustrations of each barrier. Opacity: Zhang and Zhang, 2023.

Shre, about 1 minute 45 seconds. One card per press of next. The buttons inside each card are optional: ask why, who is responsible, use diverse data, check the patient yourself. The adult and child example under bias is illustrative.

How much to trust an AI recommendation?

Too little
Calibrated
Too much

Automation bias: trusting automation too much without using your own judgment.

Conclusions

What this means

Climbing the evidence ladder
Retrospective testing
Tested at a single centerMost models today
Tested across hospitals and patient groups
Evaluated in real-world settings
Shown to improve patient safetyWhat we need

Limits of our review

Our research was not exhaustive, and some of the studies we examined have not been independently tested.

What needs to happen

Stronger evidence that AI is reliable and benefits patients, not only that it performs well in theory.

Implication for education

AI literacy in medical education, so clinicians can critically interpret AI recommendations and avoid over-reliance.

Shre, about 1 minute 15 seconds. Ladder first: most models reviewed were tested at a single center. Next: what we need is evidence on patient safety. Then the two limits of the review and the implication. The AI literacy card is optional to read aloud, since it was covered on the previous slide.
